checkpoints: Calling `new` on dependencies inside the constructor turns the consumer into something that both uses and creates its dependencies — violating separation of concerns and becoming the root of every problem as the system scales.

It hard-wires the consumer to one concrete implementation, forcing you to edit the consumer to swap it (tight coupling); an IoC container reverses this — the consumer only declares the type it needs, so implementations can be swapped without touching the consumer (loose coupling).

Because the dependency is created inside the constructor, tests are bound to the real object and no mock/stub can be injected to isolate the unit; an IoC container reverses this by letting a mock/stub be injected from outside, giving natural testability.

Every `new` yields a separate copy, losing sharing — no shared state or expensive resource; an IoC container reverses this because it owns the lifecycle and can share a single instance (e.g. a singleton) across consumers.
Once the dependency graph grows, hand-wiring the correct initialization order becomes fragile and brittle.

Letting an IoC container create and wire things instead: the consumer only declares "I need a CatService" via the constructor parameter type; the container reads that type, builds the dependency graph, creates instances in the right order, and injects them — solving the fragile-ordering problem too.
This reversal — the power to create objects moving from the consumer to the container — is exactly what inversion of control means.

The lifecycle is a pipeline with three axes — inbound (Middleware → Guard → Interceptor-before → Pipe), business (Handler runs), and outbound (Interceptor-after before the response leaves) — plus a separate error-escape path, not a flat list of side-by-side steps.
Middleware runs earliest, before the framework even knows which Handler will handle the request — it only does raw cross-cutting work like attaching a request-id or writing an access log.

Guard answers "may this request pass?" — it sees the Handler plus its metadata (via a Reflector, e.g. `@Roles`) to decide continue vs. reject with 401/403; it sits before Pipe because authorization is cheap and must reject earliest, before more expensive layers do any work.

Pipe answers "is the input valid?" — it validates and transforms each parameter's type and value, throwing 400 on failure, so the Handler always receives clean, correctly-typed data instead of littering itself with defensive `if` checks.

Interceptor answers "what wraps around the Handler?" — it's the ONLY layer that wraps both directions: before measures timing before the Handler runs, after transforms the returned value via `map`; only it can compute something spanning the entire call (like a total `executionMs`) or normalize the final response.

Exception filter answers "where do errors jump?" — it does not sit on that sequential line: a `throw` from any layer, anywhere in the chain, makes the flow jump straight to the filter and skip every remaining layer, so it's centralized error handling rather than one more link.

The framework fixes this exact order deliberately, not arbitrarily: each layer only has exactly the context it needs, exactly when it needs it, so putting a concern in the wrong layer forces that layer to simulate context it was never meant to have.

A per-handler try/catch that builds its own JSON error response duplicates work already owned by the framework's centralized error-handling layer (an exception filter on Nest/Spring/ASP.NET, or a central middleware plus recover() on Go) — the entire reason that layer exists is to define ONE response envelope for the whole system.

When every handler catches its own errors, the response shape drifts across endpoints — one returns {message}, another returns {error, detail} — forcing clients to guess the format per endpoint instead of parsing a single contract.

Returning an exception's raw message straight to the client violates hide-by-default: that message belongs to whatever exception fired underneath — a DB driver, an ORM — and can carry table names, column names, or query fragments that must never reach outside the server.

Catching an expected domain error such as "not found" inside a local try/catch collapses it into the same generic response as any other failure, throwing away the information that would let it surface as a real 404 instead of a 500.
Swallowing an error without logging it removes any trace of the failure; when a genuinely unexpected error hits production, there is nothing left to grep for, so observability is effectively gone.

The correct fix is to strip the local try/catch out of the handlers entirely: throw a typed exception (NotFoundException, BadRequestException, or an equivalent typed error/sentinel per stack) for expected cases with a message the domain deliberately chose to expose, and let everything else fall through to the one centralized handler that already classifies, logs, and formats it.

Separating a MUST-FIX (an information leak, lost observability) from a mere style preference matters because the error envelope is a consistency contract every consumer of the API relies on, not a matter of per-handler taste.

The fix can be verified with a test that throws a domain error inside the service, calls the endpoint, asserts the response matches the centralized handler's standard envelope ({statusCode, error, message, timestamp, path}), and asserts the body contains none of the original internal driver or ORM message text.

A single log-heavy endpoint can carry three distinct costs at once — CPU-bound formatting, I/O-bound blocking, and allocation-bound serialization — and each needs to be isolated and measured on its own before any fix is applied, because changing all three together leaves no way to know which one actually mattered.

Colorized, pretty-printed log output (colorize()/nestLike-style formatting) exists for a human reading a terminal during development; in production nobody watches a live terminal, so the service should emit plain single-line structured JSON and push any prettifying work to the reader side — a log viewer or aggregator like Loki/Grafana — instead of spending CPU on it in the request path.

A logging transport that calls a synchronous file-write function (like fs.appendFileSync) on every log call blocks the thread or event loop handling that request until the disk write completes, so a log-heavy endpoint effectively becomes I/O-starved on every request.

The fix for a synchronous file-write transport is to switch to an async or buffered writer, or more simply to drop the homegrown file transport entirely and write to stdout so a collector or sidecar (such as Fluentd or Vector) can ship the logs — either way the service stops waiting on disk.

Logging the full request and response body at info level on every single request is the largest serialization and payload cost of the three, since most successful requests never need their full body to debug; the fix is a level policy that keeps full-body logging only on the error path, sampling a fraction of normal requests, or an allow-list that logs just the handful of fields that matter.

After applying fixes, a before/after load test that re-measures p99 latency and CPU is the only way to confirm the change produced a real improvement, and the same check should verify that log volume hasn't been cut so far that it now hurts debugging.

Every reduction in logging detail trades away some real debugging power, so the honest, sustainable split is to keep full detail on the error path — where an investigation is actually needed — and trim only the happy path, rather than cutting evenly everywhere.
NestJS providers default to singleton scope: one instance is built at bootstrap and shared across every request, which is cheap and sufficient as long as the provider is stateless.

Declaring a provider `Scope.REQUEST` propagates upward through the dependency graph — any provider that depends on it, directly or transitively, is forced into request scope too and loses its singleton lifetime, even if its own code never changed.

In this code, marking `TenantContext` as request-scoped to hold per-request `tenantId` drags `LoggerService` and then `OrderService` into request scope as well, purely because they sit on the chain leading back to it.

The real cost of the regression is not the business logic (`createOrder`'s save call is untouched) but the fact that the entire affected chain of instances now has to be re-constructed and re-resolved on every single request instead of being reused from a shared singleton.

This repeated construction and resolution work is exactly what produces the observed doubling of p99 latency and the 40% throughput drop, since more CPU and allocation work happens per request with no change in what that request actually does.
If a request-scoped provider sits inside the request pipeline itself, such as a guard or interceptor, the same propagation spreads even wider and the performance cost grows correspondingly larger.

The fix is to carry per-request tenant context through an execution-scoped storage mechanism instead of provider scope: AsyncLocalStorage in Node, ThreadLocal in Java, AsyncLocal<T> in C#, or explicit `context.Context` threading in Go all let contextual data travel across async boundaries without making the provider (or anything depending on it) request-scoped, so the whole chain reverts to singleton.

Request scope is genuinely justified only when per-request state absolutely must never leak or mix across requests and no other isolation mechanism exists; using it merely as a convenient way to carry contextual data is what silently propagates reconstruction cost through the dependency graph, as it does here.

Fixing the scope alone is not sufficient proof of resolution — the fix should be validated by re-running the same load profile used to surface the regression and confirming that p99 latency and throughput actually return to baseline, not just that the diff looks cleaner on review.

The root problem is free-form string logging: it has no fields, so an aggregator (Loki/ELK) must regex-guess each part and breaks the instant the message wording changes — it can't answer "every log with `level=error` for `requestId=X` in the last 5 minutes".

Structured logging: each log entry is a record with fields (`level`, `message`, `context`, `timestamp`, plus `requestId`/`userId`) serialized as one-line JSON, so machines can index and filter by field.

Transport fan-out: the logger holds several outputs and pushes one event to every output, each with its own format chain — one destination prints colored lines for devs to skim on the terminal, another emits plain JSON for the aggregator.

Why not force a single format: with only one format either devs suffer (reading raw JSON by eye) or machines suffer (parsing ANSI-colored strings); fan-out gives the same data two presentations without calling log twice.

A unified logger merges framework/runtime-internal logs (route mapping, lifecycle, errors) and application logs into one pipeline, so a single `requestId` runs end-to-end from route match to business event and the trace isn't broken at the framework/app boundary.

Don't enable pretty format on the file/production sink, because the aggregator would swallow ANSI codes and fail to parse, and it wastes CPU — each transport gets the format right for its destination.

Every error from every layer should converge on ONE central error-handling point — in the request lifecycle this point sits "off the straight line", so any layer that produces an error makes the flow jump straight there, skipping the rest; the exact mechanism differs by stack (a global exception filter/handler for exception-based frameworks like Nest/Spring/ASP.NET vs. an error-handling middleware plus `recover()` and a shared response writer for Go) but the idea is identical: exactly one exit for errors.

Because every error is guaranteed to pass through this one point, shaping the response there gives immediate system-wide consistency; if each controller catches and formats on its own, clients get a different shape per endpoint and someone eventually leaks a stack.

Expected errors (usually 4xx — not found, bad input, conflict, unauthenticated) belong to the client: their message is written deliberately by the domain, so it's safe for the client to read and the central point keeps it as-is.

Unexpected errors (5xx — a programming error, DB down, broken invariant) belong to the server: their real message carries a stack/SQL string that's unsafe to expose, so the central point replaces it with a generic message and pushes the real stack only into internal logs for on-call.

Safe-by-default: the final catch-all/panic-recovery branch is the last net, so even a never-anticipated new error type is automatically hidden — hiding is the default behavior, exposing is the exception you must declare deliberately.
Doing the reverse — exposing by default and remembering to hide each error type — means forgetting one branch leaks internals, and you can never be sure you've hidden them all.

The envelope is a contract — `{statusCode, error, message, timestamp, path}` (ideally plus `requestId`) — that lets the caller write one error-handling code path instead of guessing the shape per endpoint.
`path` and `timestamp` are not decoration: they map a client's error report to the exact server log line, turning a vague "the API returned 500" into a traceable incident.
The error fires at bootstrap, not at request time, because Nest always finishes building the dependency graph before the app starts.
`WalletService` is registered in `WalletModule`'s `providers`, but `WalletModule` never `exports` it.

`CheckoutModule` has `imports: [WalletModule]`, but `imports` only grants access to whatever the other module actively opened via `exports` — `WalletService` isn't on that public surface, so the container can't resolve it for `CheckoutService`.
The correct fix is just adding `exports: [WalletService]` to `WalletModule`; `CheckoutModule` and `CheckoutService`'s constructor stay untouched.

Adding `WalletService` to `CheckoutModule`'s own `providers` to "make the error go away" is wrong, because Nest treats that as an independent registration — each module has its own provider scope — so two separate `WalletService` instances now exist side by side.

One `CheckoutService` debits from, and one `WalletModule` still reads the balance from — the app stops complaining at bootstrap, but the shared state is gone and the balance goes wrong with no exception to point at it, far harder to catch than the loud resolve error at startup.
General principle: `providers` decides where an instance gets created; `exports`/`imports` decides who gets to share that exact same instance.
Identifies this as the classic "wrong profile picked" bug, rooted in misunderstanding the precedence model.
Explains first-match-wins: in NestJS ConfigModule with envFilePath, the file list is a priority order — for each key, the value in the first file found is used, and later files do NOT override.

Explains the two models are directly opposite about "who wins", giving merge/override contrast examples — ASP.NET Core (appsettings.json + appsettings.{env}.json, later source wins), Spring (base + application-{profile}.yml merge), and Go/Viper's precedence chain (flag > env > file > default).
Explains the general mechanism of the bug: it happens when a developer thinks they're in one model but are actually in the other, ordering the files wrong.
Gives the concrete example: if .env.production sits ahead of .env.staging in a first-match-wins array, staging still reads production values for every shared key.
Notes the danger is that it's silent: no compile error, no exception, the app boots normally — only the values are wrong, exactly "right 95%, silently wrong 5%".
Gives the immediate fix: print/re-read the actual envFilePath order in the running instance, confirm the correct-environment file is first, fix the order.
Gives the long-term fix: add schema validation at bootstrap so a mismatched profile fails fast instead of silently running wrong.
States that validating inside the service is too late — fail-fast means rejecting invalid input at the boundary before spending effort on it.
States that in the request lifecycle, the validation layer (pipe) runs before the handler, so invalid input is rejected early and never reaches business logic.
Gives a concrete example of wasted work when validation happens late (e.g., a transaction already opened, the DB already queried, or another service already called before the bad input is caught).
States that this late-caught work burns server resources (CPU/IO) on effort that is guaranteed to be discarded.
States that the validation layer does not just check input but also transforms it (e.g., converts it to the correct type), not merely rejects it.
States that the handler's own code becomes simpler once it can assume the input is already valid — fewer defensive checks and branches.

Frames the split as separation of concerns / single responsibility: validation belongs in the layer that has direct visibility into each parameter's type and value, and pushing it into the service duplicates that work per handler.
